name: Vesugen

angle.text: Longevity users take Vesugen as a vascular peptide, with the hope that better blood vessel health feeds into a younger overall look. The appearance link is a theory users draw; evidence is cell-culture work and one small Russian human report, with no appearance testing.

summary: A Lys-Glu-Asp tripeptide (KED) from Khavinson's lab pitched for blood vessels; cell-culture data, one small Russian human report, no appearance link.
note: Research peptide; evidence is mostly in vitro and from one research network.
currentQuick:
Vesugen is a three-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as a vascular-protective agent.
Studies are mostly cell cultures. A Russian patent exists for a capillary-strengthening use, but no controlled human trial was found.
How it works: Reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged vascular cell cultures, apparently by interacting with its gene promoter in docking models [1]. Also reported to limit lipid peroxidation of lipoproteins in vitro [2].
Risks and caveats: No systematic human safety data; not an approved medicine.
deepLead:
Vesugen is a synthetic tripeptide, Lys-Glu-Asp (KED, also called T-38), developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group and described as a vasoprotective peptide based on sequences from vascular-tissue extracts .
Published work is mostly in vitro: it was reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged endothelial and tissue cultures  and to restrict lipid peroxidation of human lipoproteins . A Russian-language report examined synthetic peptides in elderly patients with brain syndrome . It is not an approved drug and no appearance use is documented.

name: Crystagen

angle.text: Crystagen is used in peptide-bioregulator circles as an immune and spleen peptide for ageing. Users sometimes fold it into broader anti-ageing stacks, but the appearance link is a loose theory; support consists of small lab reports, with nothing on looks.

summary: A Russian three-amino-acid 'bioregulator' peptide with spleen and immune claims backed only by small lab reports.
note: No human trials found; research-peptide status.
currentQuick:
Crystagen is a tripeptide from the Khavinson family of short peptide bioregulators, discussed in a Russian paper as an immune-supporting peptide for the ageing spleen.
The literature is small and mostly from the developing group. No human trial exists, and it has no documented role in appearance.
How it works: The cited paper reports that it activates B-cells in the spleen of ageing animals, alongside related peptides that act on T-helpers.
Risks and caveats: No safety data in humans was found. It is sold as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Crystagen is a short synthetic peptide with the sequence Thr-Lys-Glu (TKE, also written EDP in some listings), one of the "Khavinson peptides" developed in Russia as so-called peptide bioregulators. It is described in the literature as an immunoprotective peptide whose reported actions concern the spleen and the immune system during ageing.
The published material consists of a small number of laboratory and animal studies, largely from the St. Petersburg group that developed these peptides. A 2014 paper in a Russian gerontology journal reports that Crystagen, alongside the related peptides Vilon, Timogen and R-1, has immunoprotective effects in the ageing spleen, and that Crystagen activates B-cells. No human clinical trials were found, and no study has examined it for an appearance purpose.

name: Chonluten

angle.text: Chonluten is promoted in peptide-bioregulator communities as a lung and airway mucosa peptide. It is used for respiratory health rather than a specific look; evidence is cell-line data, and no appearance use has been studied.

summary: A tripeptide from the Khavinson 'bioregulator' family said to support respiratory mucosa, with only cell-line data.
note: Cell-culture evidence only; no human trials found.
currentQuick:
Chonluten is a three-amino-acid peptide (Glu-Asp-Gly) from the Khavinson peptide family, associated with the lining of the airways.
The only evidence found is a 2022 cell-line study; it has no documented appearance use.
How it works: In the cited experiment, it was tested alongside other Khavinson peptides for effects on proliferation and inflammatory pathways in cultured monocyte/macrophage cells.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data was found. It is sold as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Chonluten is a short synthetic peptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Gly (EDG), one of the Khavinson peptides that are marketed under the term peptide bioregulators. It is described as a regulator of the respiratory mucosa.
Published evidence found is limited to cell-culture work: a 2022 study in a human monocyte/macrophage cell line tested Chonluten together with Epitalon, Vilon, Thymogen and Thymalin for effects on proliferation and inflammatory pathways. No human clinical trial was found, and no study addresses appearance.

name: Livagen

angle.text: Forum posters pitch Livagen as a peptide that makes cells look and act younger, and treat bioregulators as a non-injectable anti-ageing option. Lab data covers chromatin in old-donor cells; the step to visible ageing is untested in humans.

summary: A Russian four-amino-acid 'bioregulator' peptide with lab data on old-donor chromatin and no human appearance data.
note: Cell and animal evidence only; sold as a research peptide.
currentQuick:
Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala, KEDA) is a short peptide from the Khavinson group in Russia, described as a regulator of gene activity in ageing cells.
Published studies are small and mostly in cultured lymphocytes and rats. A looksmax.org guide presents it as a youth-promoting peptide, but nothing published tests skin, hair or bone in people.
How it works: Researchers report that it decondenses heterochromatin and activates ribosomal genes in lymphocytes from older donors, and stimulates liver tissue growth in culture.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data was found. It is sold online as a research peptide rather than as an approved medicine.
deepLead:
Livagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala (KEDA), developed in Russia as one of the short peptide bioregulators associated with Vladimir Khavinson and the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology.
Its published research is mainly laboratory work on chromatin in lymphocytes from elderly donors, along with rat studies on tissue growth and digestive enzymes. Authors report that it activates ribosomal genes and loosens condensed heterochromatin. No controlled human trials of its effects on appearance or ageing were found. On forums it is occasionally described as a way to keep gene expression youthful, a claim not tested in published studies of skin, hair or bone.

name: Thymalin

angle.text: Thymalin is a calf-thymus extract used in Russia as an immune drug and promoted for longevity. Looksmaxxing interest is a general anti-ageing hope; the data comes mostly from its developers, with no appearance outcomes measured.

summary: A Russian calf-thymus peptide extract sold as an immune and longevity drug, with data mostly from its developers.
note: Animal-derived extract; evidence largely from one research group.
currentQuick:
Thymalin is a calf-thymus extract developed in Russia as an immune-modulating drug and promoted within a family of 'bioregulator' peptides for ageing.
Support comes mostly from animal studies and reports by its developers. It has no documented appearance use.
How it works: Proponents say its thymic peptides activate T-cell differentiation and restore immune function; Thymogen (Glu-Trp) and Vilon were derived from it.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not describe human adverse effects. It is an animal-derived preparation, and legal status varies by country.
deepLead:
Thymalin is a Russian pharmaceutical preparation made by mild acid extraction of calf thymus. It was put into practice there as an immunocorrector, a drug meant to modulate immune function.
From it the same research group isolated the dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp, later sold as Thymogen, and designed the synthetic dipeptide Vilon. Thymalin is also grouped with Epithalamin in the Khavinson program on peptides and ageing. Evidence is mainly from animal and cell studies; this entry's sources include no randomized trial of Thymalin for appearance.

name: Epithalamin

angle.text: Epithalamin, the pineal extract behind Epitalon, is used by longevity enthusiasts hoping to slow ageing, including how old someone looks. Lifespan data exists in flies and rodents; human trials and appearance measures are absent.

summary: The bovine pineal extract behind Epitalon, with lifespan data in flies and rodents but no human trials.
note: Animal-derived; data largely from its developers.
currentQuick:
Epithalamin is a pineal-gland peptide extract developed in Russia, from which the tetrapeptide Epitalon was derived.
Animal studies from the developing group report longer lifespan in flies, mice and rats. It has no documented appearance use and no randomized human trial was found.
How it works: Proposed actions include raising pineal melatonin output and antioxidant effects; these are reported in animals.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data was not found in the sources reviewed. It is an animal-derived preparation not approved in most countries.
deepLead:
Epithalamin is a peptide preparation extracted from the pineal gland of cattle, developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia. The synthetic tetrapeptide Epitalon was later derived from it.
Studies from the group report that it lengthened lifespan in fruit flies, mice and rats, and that it raised melatonin production in old rats. Most evidence is animal data from the same group. No randomized controlled trial in humans was found among the sources reviewed.

name: Cortexin

angle.text: Cortexin is a cattle-brain peptide medicine used mainly in Russia for neurological conditions. It appears in biohacking lists as a nootropic-style option; local trials address neurology, and no appearance use is documented.

summary: A Russian cattle-brain peptide injection used for neurological conditions, with some local trials and no appearance data.
note: Animal-derived injectable; regional prescription drug.
currentQuick:
Cortexin is a cattle-brain-cortex peptide complex made by Geropharm and prescribed in Russia and nearby countries for neurological conditions.
It is occasionally described as a nootropic, but has no documented use for appearance. Evidence is a Russian randomized study and rat ischemia models.
How it works: It is proposed to act as a neuroprotective and neurotrophic peptide mixture; an animal study showed protective effects in brain ischemia.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give limited safety information. It is an animal-derived injectable available by prescription in Russia.
deepLead:
Cortexin is a neuroprotective peptide medicine made by the Russian company Geropharm from the cerebral cortex of cattle. It is given by intramuscular injection and used mainly in Russia and some post-Soviet countries for neurological conditions such as cerebrovascular disorders, head injury effects, encephalopathies and developmental delay in children.
A rat study found neuroprotective activity in models of brain ischemia, and a Russian multicenter randomized study examined dose-dependent effects in chronic cerebral ischemia. Cochrane's review of the related product Cerebrolysin, not Cortexin, addresses acute stroke. No evidence was found of any appearance use; it is sometimes discussed as a nootropic.

name: Retinalamin

angle.text: Retinalamin is an animal-derived retinal peptide used clinically in Russia for glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. It is discussed in longevity circles for eye health; it has been studied for those retinal conditions, and no cosmetic eye use is documented.

summary: Animal-derived retinal peptide extract from Russia, studied in glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy; no appearance use is documented.
note: Evidence is mostly Russian-language studies from the developer's research network; not an appearance product.
currentQuick:
Retinalamin is a peptide extract made from animal retinas, developed in Russia by Vladimir Khavinson's group. It is used there by injection for eye conditions such as glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy.
It shows up in longevity-peptide lists next to other Khavinson preparations. No studies examine it for appearance.
How it works: Its developers describe it as a tissue-specific peptide complex that supports retinal cells. Cell-culture work reports stimulation of retinal and pigment epithelial cell proliferation.
Risks and caveats: Published safety data come mainly from Russian studies by the developer's network. It is not approved as a drug in most Western countries, and independent Western trials are not documented.
deepLead:
Retinalamin is a polypeptide extract prepared from the retinas of cattle or pigs. It was developed in Russia within the group of gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and belongs to the family of animal-tissue-derived peptide preparations that this group calls cytomedins or peptide bioregulators . It is used clinically in Russia and neighbouring countries, mainly by injection, for retinal conditions such as glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy .
Published human research consists largely of Russian-language studies in the journal Vestnik oftalmologii, in which Retinalamin was given alongside standard care to people with glaucoma whose eye pressure was already controlled. These reports describe improvements in some structural and functional measures compared with control groups . Laboratory studies describe effects on retinal and pigment epithelial cell proliferation in culture .
Retinalamin is not an appearance product. It appears in longevity-peptide discussions because it is listed together with other Khavinson preparations such as Epithalamin and Prostatilen . Much of the supporting literature comes from the developer's own research network, and the review summarising it was written by the same group .

name: Prostatilen

angle.text: Prostatilen is a bovine prostate extract used in post-Soviet urology for prostatitis and prostate enlargement. It appears in bioregulator discussions as a general-health option; data is mostly Russian-language clinical work, with no appearance use.

summary: Bovine prostate peptide extract used in post-Soviet urology; mostly Russian-language data and no appearance use.
note: Evidence is regional and largely from the developers' network; not an appearance product.
currentQuick:
Prostatilen is a peptide extract from cattle prostate, developed in the Soviet Union and used in Russia and nearby countries for prostatitis and prostate enlargement.
It is listed with other Khavinson peptide bioregulators in longevity circles. No studies examine it for appearance.
How it works: Its developers describe a tissue-specific effect on the prostate. Rat studies report changes in prostate size and oxidative-stress markers.
Risks and caveats: Safety information comes mostly from regional studies; two older mouse studies examined mutagenicity. It is not a Western-approved drug, and independent trials are not documented.
deepLead:
Prostatilen is a peptide preparation extracted from the prostate glands of cattle. It was developed in the Soviet Union in the mid-1980s and has been used in Russia, Ukraine and other post-Soviet countries for chronic prostatitis and benign prostatic hyperplasia, according to Grokipedia . It belongs to the family of organ-derived peptide bioregulators, or cytomedins, associated with Vladimir Khavinson's research group .
Published human studies are largely Russian-language reports from the early 1990s on prostatitis, plus experimental work in rats and mice . A 2026 paper examined prostate-derived complex peptide preparations and erectile function in men with chronic prostatitis . No Western randomised trials are listed in the available literature.
Prostatilen is a urology product rather than a cosmetic one. It appears in longevity-peptide discussions alongside other Khavinson preparations .

name: Cortagen

angle.text: Cortagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide modelled on Cortexin and proposed as a brain-tissue regulator in ageing. Interest is in cognition and longevity; it has been studied in cells and animals, with no appearance evidence.

summary: Khavinson brain-derived tetrapeptide (AEDP) studied only in cells and animals; no appearance evidence.
note: Research is mostly from the developers' laboratory; not an appearance product.
currentQuick:
Cortagen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro) made by Vladimir Khavinson's Russian group, modelled on a brain-cortex peptide extract called Cortexin.
Studies are limited to cells, rodents and a few small reports. No human trial for appearance exists.
How it works: Its developers propose that short peptides regulate gene expression in a tissue-specific way. Studies report changes in gene and interleukin-2 expression in cell and animal models.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data are essentially absent from the published literature, and it is not an approved drug in Western countries.
deepLead:
Cortagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro, made by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia from the amino-acid analysis of Cortexin, a natural brain-cortex peptide preparation . It is one of the short synthetic peptide bioregulators the group proposes as tissue-specific regulators of ageing-related changes .
Published work consists of cell-culture, animal and small biochemical studies, many from the developers' laboratory. They examined gene expression in mouse heart , interleukin-2 expression , sciatic nerve regeneration  and free-radical processes . One Russian report compared Cortexin and Cortagen in brain function in chronic ischaemia .
It is not an appearance product and no published trial in healthy people examines it.

name: Ovagen

angle.text: Ovagen is a Khavinson tripeptide described as acting on the liver and digestive tract. It is mentioned in longevity peptide lists for organ support; published human data is thin, and no appearance use is described.

summary: Khavinson liver-targeted tripeptide (EDL) with essentially no verifiable published human data and no appearance use.
note: Very thin sourcing; not an appearance product.
currentQuick:
Ovagen is a three-amino-acid peptide (Glu-Asp-Leu) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia and described as targeting liver and gut tissue.
Verified published studies on it are scarce, and none address appearance.
How it works: Its developers propose that short peptides bind DNA and regulate gene expression; this has not been confirmed independently.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data could be verified. It is sold as a research compound or supplement and is not an approved drug in most countries.
deepLead:
Ovagen is a synthetic tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Leu (EDL), developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia as part of its Cytogen family of short peptides, according to Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia . It is described there as investigated for effects on the liver and gastrointestinal tract and as modulating gene expression in a tissue-specific way .
The same source states that evidence is limited to animal models, cell cultures and studies from Russian institutions, that no large Western randomised trials exist, and that it is marketed as a research compound or supplement rather than an approved drug . Verified peer-reviewed human studies of Ovagen could not be identified.

name: Pancragen

angle.text: Pancragen is a Khavinson tetrapeptide designed to target pancreatic tissue, used in bioregulator circles for metabolic and ageing support. Evidence spans cells, animals and one small human study, with no appearance outcomes.

summary: Khavinson pancreas-targeted tetrapeptide with cell, animal and one small human study; no appearance evidence.
note: Evidence is from the developers' group; not an appearance product.
currentQuick:
Pancragen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia, aimed at pancreatic tissue.
Studies cover cell cultures, rats, monkeys and a single small human report on glucose metabolism. None address appearance.
How it works: Its developers report that it raises expression of pancreatic cell differentiation factors in culture, which they propose underlies metabolic effects.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data are very limited, and it is not an approved drug in Western countries.
deepLead:
Pancragen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp, usually amidated) developed by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, designed to target pancreatic tissue . It belongs to the short synthetic peptide bioregulators the group proposes as tissue-specific regulators in ageing .
Research includes cell cultures showing that it raises expression of differentiation factors in pancreatic cells , streptozotocin-diabetic rats , aged rhesus monkeys  and one small study in older people with and without type 2 diabetes . The human study reported lower fasting glucose and insulin resistance index in treated patients .
It is not an appearance product. Nearly all published work comes from the developing group.

name: Prostamax

angle.text: Prostamax is a Khavinson tetrapeptide modelled on the prostate extract Prostatilen and used for prostate support. It is discussed in longevity peptide communities; evidence is cell and rat-tissue work, with no appearance use.

summary: A four-amino-acid Russian "bioregulator" peptide tied to prostate support; only cell and rat-tissue work exists.
note: No human trials; unregulated research-chemical product.
currentQuick:
Prostamax is a four-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro) from the Khavinson group in St. Petersburg, part of a family of short bioregulator peptides marketed for aging and organ-specific support. Its supposed target is the prostate.
Published work is limited to cultured cells and rat tissue, mostly from the developers' circle. No human trials were found, and its link to appearance is indirect.
How it works: Proponents propose that the peptide enters cell nuclei and loosens condensed chromatin, changing gene expression. This has been reported in lymphocytes from elderly donors in vitro.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data from trials were found. It has no regulatory approval for human use and is sold as a research chemical, so product purity is not assured.
deepLead:
Prostamax is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro (KEDP), developed by Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as one of a series of short-peptide "bioregulators" . It was designed around the amino acid composition of Prostatilen, a prostate-tissue extract preparation, and is described by its developers as acting on prostate tissue .
Published work on Prostamax consists of cell-culture and animal experiments plus in vitro studies of lymphocytes from elderly donors, mostly from the Khavinson group and collaborators, reporting effects on chromatin structure . No clinical trials were found. In looksmaxxing and longevity circles it appears as a niche "research peptide" in the same family as Epithalon.

name: Testagen

angle.text: Testagen is promoted in research-peptide and longevity communities as supporting testicular function and testosterone, which users link to muscle, leanness and masculine features. The claim is based on developer material, and human evidence is absent.

summary: A four-amino-acid "bioregulator" peptide pitched for testosterone support, with no human evidence behind it.
note: No human studies; sold as research chemical.
currentQuick:
Testagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly) is a short peptide in the Khavinson bioregulator family, promoted for testicular and testosterone support.
The only published work found shows that such peptides can enter cultured cells, plus an unrelated corrosion-chemistry paper. No studies in people exist.
How it works: Proponents suggest short peptides enter nuclei and interact with DNA to alter gene expression; this has been shown only as cell uptake in culture.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data were found. It is not an approved medicine and is sold unregulated as a research chemical.
deepLead:
Testagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly (KEDG), part of the family of short "bioregulator" peptides associated with Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia . It is promoted in research-peptide and longevity communities as supporting testicular function and testosterone.
Evidence is very thin. A laboratory study showed that fluorescent-labeled short peptides including Testagen can enter cells and nuclei in culture , and a 2025 materials-science paper examined Testagen as a copper-corrosion inhibitor . No studies of Testagen in people were found.

name: Thymulin

angle.text: Thymulin is a thymus hormone that needs zinc to be active, and appears in peptide and zinc discussions. Human data covers zinc status and thymic function, not supplement use, and no appearance use has been studied.

summary: A zinc-dependent thymic peptide hormone; human data cover zinc status, not use as a supplement or for looks.
note: No clinical trials as a treatment; research-chemical sales.
currentQuick:
Thymulin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made by the thymus that needs zinc to be active. It has been studied for immune and neuroendocrine roles.
It is sold as a research peptide in longevity circles, but no trials of it as a treatment, and none for appearance, were found.
How it works: It is thought to promote T-cell maturation and temper inflammatory signaling, with activity depending on zinc binding.
Risks and caveats: No human safety trials of the peptide were found. It is not an approved drug and is sold unregulated.
deepLead:
Thymulin, also called facteur thymique sérique (FTS) or serum thymic factor, is a nine-amino-acid peptide (pGlu-Ala-Lys-Ser-Gln-Gly-Gly-Ser-Asn) produced by the thymus and requiring zinc for biological activity . It was described by Jean-Francois Bach and colleagues in 1977 .
Research has concerned its role in T-cell differentiation, neuroendocrine regulation and inflammation . It is sold by some vendors as a research peptide in longevity circles, but no human trials of thymulin as a treatment were found, and it has no recognized appearance use.

name: Thymosin Beta-4

chain: Tissue repair and hair follicle signalling
angle.text: Sold as TB-500, thymosin beta-4 is used by lifters for tissue recovery and by hair-loss hobbyists hoping for follicle effects. Human trials cover wounds and eyes; hair data is from mice, and appearance use in people is untested.

summary: A natural actin-binding peptide with wound and eye trials and mouse hair data; sold as TB-500, banned in sport.
note: Not approved; no human hair trials; WADA-prohibited.
currentQuick:
Thymosin beta-4 is a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide that regulates actin in cells. Phase 2 trials tested it for skin ulcers and eye conditions, with mixed or incomplete results reported.
Hair-growth claims rest on mouse studies. It circulates online as a research peptide, along with the fragment TB-500.
How it works: It binds monomeric actin to control cell structure and movement, and is reported to promote cell migration and new blood vessels outside cells.
Risks and caveats: Trials reported mild effects, but long-term data are lacking. Its blood-vessel-promoting activity raises theoretical tumor concerns. It is unapproved, WADA-prohibited, and gray-market products vary in purity.
deepLead:
Thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) is a small, abundant peptide of about 43 amino acids, encoded by the TMSB4X gene, whose best-established role is binding monomeric actin and thereby regulating the cell cytoskeleton . It was first isolated from calf thymus and sequenced in 1981 by the group of Allan Goldstein.
Outside cells it has been reported to promote cell migration, blood-vessel formation and tissue repair . Phase 2 trials have tested it in skin ulcers, epidermolysis bullosa, dry eye and corneal wounds, and cardiac trials were registered . In looksmaxxing and recovery communities it is discussed mainly as a hair-growth and healing "research peptide", with a related fragment sold as TB-500. Hair findings come from mouse studies, and no approved use exists .

name: Thymosin Fraction 5

angle.text: Thymosin fraction 5 is the calf-thymus extract from which thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were purified. It matters here as the origin of those peptides rather than as a product people use for looks; no appearance use is documented.

summary: The calf-thymus extract that thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were purified from; relevant here only as their source.
note: Mixture; no approved use or appearance data.
currentQuick:
Thymosin fraction 5 is a calf-thymus extract made in 1972 that contains dozens of peptides. Thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were later purified from it.
It has no appearance evidence; clinical studies concern purified thymosin alpha-1 in infection and cancer.
How it works: The extract restored immune function in thymus-deficient animals, which led to the idea of thymic hormones; individual peptides have different actions.
Risks and caveats: No approved use of the extract was found, and no appearance-related safety data. Animal-derived mixtures vary in composition.
deepLead:
Thymosin fraction 5 (TF5) is a partially purified extract of calf thymus prepared in 1972 by Allan Goldstein's group, which contains many small peptides, including the later-characterized thymosin alpha-1 and thymosin beta-4 . It was the starting material from which individual thymosins were purified.
Its relevance to looksmaxxing is indirect: it appears in thymic peptide and longevity discussions as the origin of the peptides sold as research chemicals. Published clinical work focuses on purified thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) in infection and cancer, not on TF5 for appearance .

name: Thymopentin

angle.text: Thymopentin is an immune peptide used in some countries for infections and studied in skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis and eczema. Appearance interest is an extension of that skin-disease work; trials on cosmetic outcomes do not exist.

summary: A thymus-derived immune peptide studied for infections and skin disease, with no appearance trials behind it.
note: Studied as an immune drug; no appearance or longevity outcomes have been tested.
currentQuick:
Thymopentin is a five-amino-acid peptide based on the thymus hormone thymopoietin. It is classed as an immunostimulant and has been tested in HIV, atopic dermatitis, cancer and other immune-related conditions.
It appears in peptide and longevity discussion as an immune-modulating compound. No published trial has tested it for an appearance outcome.
How it works: It is described as interacting with T cells, with binding to HLA-DR molecules reported in one study. Much recent work concerns delivery systems because peptides are poorly absorbed orally.
Risks and caveats: Safety information was not covered in the sources reviewed. Its regulatory status varies by country, and it is not an approved appearance treatment.
deepLead:
Thymopentin (also abbreviated TP5) is a synthetic pentapeptide made of the amino acids arginine, lysine, aspartate, valine and tyrosine, derived from the thymus hormone thymopoietin. It is classed as an immunostimulant (ATC code L03AX09) and is described as interacting with T cells.
Its place in appearance and longevity discussion is peripheral: it is mentioned as an immunomodulating peptide rather than a cosmetic agent. Published human research has concentrated on immune-related conditions, including early HIV-era studies, atopic dermatitis and cancer, and no trial of it for an appearance outcome was found.

name: GHRP-3

angle.text: GHRP-3 is one of the numbered growth hormone-releasing peptides, discussed by physique enthusiasts as a way to raise GH for muscle and leanness. It is known mainly from anti-doping lists; human training or appearance trials have not been reported.

summary: A little-studied growth hormone-releasing peptide known mainly from anti-doping lists.
note: Prohibited in competitive sport; no completed human trials found.
currentQuick:
GHRP-3 is one of a numbered family of synthetic peptides that stimulate growth hormone release. It is discussed in muscle-building contexts as a growth hormone secretagogue.
Published work on it is mostly analytical chemistry for doping control. No completed human trial was found.
How it works: Like other GHRPs, it is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor.
Risks and caveats: No safety data from human trials were found. It is named on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list and is not an approved medicine.
deepLead:
GHRP-3 is a synthetic growth hormone-releasing peptide (GHRP), one of a numbered series of small peptides that act on the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor to stimulate growth hormone release. It is listed by name among the peptides prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.
The published literature on GHRP-3 specifically is very thin. It appears mainly in anti-doping analytical chemistry papers, and no completed human trial was found.

name: GHRP-4

angle.text: GHRP-4 is an obscure member of the GHRP series that physique forums mention alongside better-known secretagogues for GH-driven muscle and fat loss. It appears in anti-doping analytical papers; human trials are absent.

summary: An obscure GH-releasing peptide that shows up in anti-doping papers and nowhere in human trials.
note: Prohibited in competitive sport; no human clinical studies found.
currentQuick:
GHRP-4 belongs to a family of synthetic peptides designed to prompt growth hormone release, and is discussed in muscle-building contexts.
The published record consists of doping-control chemistry. No human clinical studies were found.
How it works: It is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor and is described as a met-enkephalin analogue.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data were found. It appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list and is not an approved medicine.
deepLead:
GHRP-4 is a synthetic growth hormone-releasing peptide in the numbered GHRP series. Analytical papers describe the GHRPs as synthetic met-enkephalin analogues containing unnatural D-amino acids, designed to stimulate growth hormone release. The family is described as orally active and capable of raising endogenous growth hormone.
GHRP-4 appears in the literature almost solely in doping-control research. No human clinical studies were found.
